evidence.claim: SR-148 has both Utah Scenic Byway and National Forest Scenic Byway designations.
evidence.quote: The entire highway has been designated the Cedar Breaks Scenic Byway as part of the Utah Scenic Byways and National Forest Scenic Byway programs.

evidence.claim: Utah’s tourism office highlights views into an amphitheater more than 2,000 feet deep and three miles across.
evidence.quote: Several easy and moderate hikes allow you to view the huge natural amphitheater, which is more than 2,000 feet deep and three miles from rim to rim.

evidence.claim: The state highway designation began in 1927 as SR-55, connecting SR-14 to the southern monument boundary.
evidence.quote: State Route 55 was designated by the Utah State Legislature in 1927, connecting SR-14 at Cedar Breaks Junction with the southern boundary of Cedar Breaks National Monument.

evidence.claim: It became part of SR-143 in 1969, but the monument road was excluded from that number, leaving two disconnected state highway sections.
evidence.quote: SR-55 was deleted in 1969, and the route was designated as part of SR-143. This left SR-143 as a non-contiguous highway, as the portion going through the national monument was not part of the highway designation.

evidence.claim: The southern section became SR-148 in 1985; the National Forest Scenic Byway designation followed in 1991.
evidence.quote: In 1985, the southern portion of SR-143 between SR-14 and the southern Cedar Breaks National Monument boundary was re-designated State Route 148

evidence.claim: The southern section became SR-148 in 1985; the National Forest Scenic Byway designation followed in 1991.

evidence.claim: For a north-to-south trip, join the monument road from SR-143 near North View.
evidence.quote: The byway continues south past the North View of Cedar Breaks where it junctions with SR-148.

evidence.claim: A large stone chimney echoes their sloping shape, and projecting logs extend beneath a cedar-shake roof.
evidence.quote: A large, battered stone chimney at one end echoes the log detailing. The roof is covered by cedar shakes, with extended log purlin ends.

flags: Route scope: cached SR-148 history ends the numbered highway at the southern monument boundary; tourism sources describe the continuing drive through the park to SR-143. Kept those scopes distinct.

Tourism sources disagree on scenic-drive distance and time: Visit Cedar City gives six miles/about 30 minutes; Visit Utah gives nine miles/15 minutes. Omitted both. The mapped 7.6 miles is context, not evidence.
Dropped current “Native people called” Circle of Painted Cliffs: cache repeats a generic attribution without naming a nation or a community source. Do not present it as a shared Indigenous name.

Historic visitor-center title and coordinates preserved. Cache describes the 1937 cabin but does not establish the current visitor-services building or its operation; text concerns historic architecture only. Its NRHP sentence mistakenly names the caretaker’s cabin, so omitted register date.

Brian Head is a northern separate excursion. Moments follow the north-to-south strip direction, then Alpine Pond/Chessman Ridge and Point Supreme. No coordinates invented for Alpine Pond. Its and Brian Head’s texts are shorter because focused cache evidence is limited.

Seasonal closure note was checked only against the saved tourism page on 2026-10-11, not live road status. Cached monument page gives a broader October–May snow-access window. No opening on the review date is asserted.
